name: Philips Lumea

lead: The Philips Lumea is a consumer handheld device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) for hair removal at home. It belongs to a category of home devices marketed as an alternative to salon or clinic treatment.

This article is short because the sources available describe the IPL category rather than this specific model. Clinical IPL generally reduces hair growth over repeated sessions, and encyclopedic sources describe it as typically less effective than laser.

paras: IPL flashes broad-spectrum light that is absorbed by melanin in the hair, heating and damaging the follicle. Only hairs in the growth phase respond, so treatments are repeated over weeks.

Reported risks of IPL include hyperpigmentation and eye injury if misused; a review of home IPL safety discussed the need for eye safety in consumer designs. Light, grey, red and white hair respond poorly.

studies.title: Are home-use intense pulsed light (IPL) devices safe?

lead: The Philips Lumea is a handheld consumer device for hair removal at home using intense pulsed light (IPL). It is one of several home IPL products sold as an alternative to treatment in a clinic.

IPL is not a laser: it uses a flashlamp emitting broad-spectrum light that is absorbed mainly by melanin in the hair follicle. [1] Encyclopedic sources describe IPL as generally less effective than laser hair removal, though many users are satisfied, and say it works best on darker, coarser hair. [1]
No sources reviewed for this article report trials of the Lumea specifically; the discussion below therefore concerns home IPL devices as a category.
infobox: Home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal device

paras: IPL devices emit light of roughly 400 to 1200 nm, filtered to block harmful ultraviolet and long infrared wavelengths; light absorbed by melanin heats and damages the follicle. [1] Only hairs in the active growth phase respond, so clinical IPL typically involves around 8 to 10 sessions several weeks apart. [1]

No studies found on the Philips Lumea specifically. Studies of other home-use IPL devices exist: a 2009 study tested a low-energy home IPL device on 34 people and 92 sites with blinded hair counts,  and a 2023 trial compared a home-use laser with a diode laser.  A 2010 paper reviewed the safety of home IPL products, noting the design challenge of making devices effective yet eye-safe. [2]

IPL complications described in encyclopedic sources include hyperpigmentation; photosensitizing medications and existing skin damage are listed as contraindications. [1] A 2010 review noted that light-based home systems are designed to cause biological damage to hair follicles and that eye safety is a central design issue. [2]
Home hair-removal devices are discussed in appearance communities as a way to reduce body and facial hair. Community sources specific to this device were not available.
